lead: Sails are checked hoisted, at the pontoon, in Saturday's calm. A fault found there is the base's to fix; found on Sunday off the headland it is your problem. See every sail up, every reef in and every furler turn before you sign.

sections.title: You sign for what you were shown

blocks.p: 'Sails: OK, checked yesterday' is not a check. Ask for the main hoisted and the genoa unrolled while it is calm. If it blows too hard, have the sail rolled out a metre and back, and write 'not fully seen' on the form.

fig.note: Both sails up at the pontoon, in light wind

head: What you find
What you ask for
rows: Chafed clew, torn leech, UV strip hanging
The base's repair before you leave
An old, stretched sail
Its state on the form; reef it early
A sail listed but not aboard; a wrong sail number
The list corrected before you sign
A gennaker on the list
Hoisted in its sock once; tack line and halyard found

blocks.p: The **inventory** you sign is what you hand back: a storm jib that was never aboard is charged as missing. A gennaker is normally outside the waiver and needs the base's written consent, so a torn one is paid in full. Report damage the day it happens: hiding it costs more than the repair.

sections.title: Up, down, and what can snag

fig.note: Walk every edge with your eyes

blocks.p: With the main up, look at every batten pocket, every luff slide and the whole leech. Missing battens let the leech flog; a cracked slide jams the hoist; a tear grows, so the sailmaker mends it before you leave, like worn spreader patches. Then let the halyard go: the sail must drop on its own, or you cannot get it down fast in a squall.

head: Halyards
What to know
rows: Tape mark at the clutch
Full hoist: stop there, or the headboard jams in the sheave
Shackle
One that can open drops the sail and sends the halyard aloft
Masthead, by binoculars
Crossed halyards are cleared from aloft, by the base
Electric winch
Short pushes, eyes on the sail, stop at any snag

blocks.p: Hoist head to wind at slow ahead, eyes aloft. If the hoist stops, a batten end is under a lazyjack: ease, clear it, go on by hand. Without lazyjacks someone flakes the sail at the mast as it drops. See a catamaran's square-top main hoisted and bagged once.

sections.title: It must roll in by hand

fig.note: Genoa fully out: this line rolls it back in

blocks.p: In light wind a furler turns by hand; one that needs a winch at the pontoon will not furl at 25 knots. The line runs fair through its lead blocks, and the sail is rolled with its **UV strip** outside. If the line goes solid, look up: the halyard may be wrapped round the forestay above the swivel. Never winch a jammed furler. Scallops along the luff ask for more halyard, just until they go.

head: At sea
What you do
rows: Furling in a breeze
Bear away so the main blankets it, keep a little sheet tension, haul by hand
The furler jams
Ease the sheet, try again by hand, call the base; cut nothing
Genoa half rolled
Move the sheet cars forward, or the leech flogs

blocks.p: Sheets show no bare core and reach their winches; each car is pinned in its track. A self-tacking jib still has one sheet, one car and two end stops to check.

sections.title: A tight roll and the boom at its mark

blocks.p: The main rolls up inside the mast through a narrow slot, where a loose roll bunches and jams. **To unfurl**, haul the outhaul on the winch while easing the furling line under slight tension. **To furl**, set the boom to the base's mark, keep a little outhaul tension and take the furling line in steadily. Never winch against a closed clutch.

fig.note: Unfurling: winch the outhaul, ease the line

blocks.rule: A bunch in the slot only tightens under power. Stop, unroll a turn, boom to its mark, furl again by hand.

sections.title: Put the reef in at the pontoon first

blocks.p: Put reef 1 in at the pontoon and try reef 2: you see which line does what, that it runs free and is long enough. Horns at the gooseneck mean a **two-line** system: someone goes to the mast, clipped on, to hook the luff cringle, then the clew line is hauled from the cockpit. A torn cringle or a short reef line is no reef: it is put right before you leave.

fig.note: The two cringles come down to the boom

blocks.p: Reefing wind speeds and a maximum wind force in the contract or the briefing are terms, not advice: sailing above them can void the insurance. The limit is read against the forecast, so you move the passage: leave before the wind arrives and tell the base. When a reef is forecast, put it in at the hoist, in flat water.

blocks.rule: Shaking a reef out is easy. Taking one in late is not.

head: Gear
What to know
rows: Mainsheet
Cracked block or worn cam cleat: replaced now. Chafed cover, sound core: noted
Rigid vang
Holds the boom up with the sail down: no topping lift
Preventer
From the boom end to the bow and back to a cockpit winch, so it can be eased
Boom brake
Slows a gybe by friction; it does not stop one
Bimini under the boom
Agree, in writing, whether it folds under sail
